title: Performance measurement and verified test scope
lead: Compare runs under the same workload and measurement conditions. A successful build, browser playback, and device execution provide different kinds of evidence.

blocks.text: Current resource use and concurrency

Local media generation chooses FFmpeg decoder, filter and video-encoder settings from available CPU allocation and estimated reclaimable memory, capped at four threads per pool. One decode supplies both video renditions and the sprite. Audio and image encoders use one thread. This is a startup budget, not an operating-system RSS or total-thread limit.

It avoids writing large raw-video intermediates to disk and reuses fragmented MP4 files across HLS, DASH, and the feature playlists. Checksumming, archive extraction, and concatenation for packet inspection read and write in one-MiB blocks. Per-Title starts and monitors three cloud jobs with fixed concurrency of three.

fixture-report.json records the detected CPU and memory resources, chosen budget and actual generation measurements. Unknown memory selects one thread. Browser correctness tests select one to four workers from available CPUs and memory, reserving one GiB and estimating two GiB per worker. E2E_WORKERS can reduce that budget. Performance measurements always use one worker. The fixed 180p/360p fixture determines the frame-memory estimate; the tool does not continuously monitor heat or resize arbitrary encoding ladders.

A separate correctness smoke run passed all ten feature checks with zero retries: one worker took 20.31 s with 2.43 GB sampled peak summed process-tree RSS; the automatic budget selected two workers and took 11.51 s with 3.70 GB. Times include server startup and shared-UI building. There was one run per mode with native qualification also running, so this records execution cost rather than a controlled speedup. Shared resident pages can be counted more than once.

Increasing the Player's forward buffer retains more media and can help tolerate temporary network interruptions. The rewind window, however, depends on the delivery manifest and media still available from the origin. A larger forward buffer cannot recover older segments already removed by the server.

React Native reads several asynchronous state values concurrently and coalesces refreshes into one running snapshot plus one pending refresh. This bounds the queue during bursts of events. Results from an old source are discarded, while a failed refresh preserves the last valid display. Live finalization and positions falling outside the rewind window are also detected from these snapshots.
Measure Web UI and playback lifecycle changes

The workload cycles through the available themes three times, changes the seek-preview setting, applies Source settings three times, recreates the Player through Player settings and live-rewind controls three times each, switches HLS/DASH three times, and finally releases the Player and UI. The 21 phases create and destroy seven Players per run. Settled states verify one active Player/media element and disposal stops the app timer.
Run the following from the repository root. Run the final media-generation command only if .cache/test-streams has not been generated. Reuse existing verified media.

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm --filter @showcase/e2e exec \
  playwright install chromium
python3 encoding/test-streams/local.py
Finish generating the media before starting a server for that directory in a separate terminal.

pnpm --filter @showcase/e2e exec vite \
  ../../.cache/test-streams \
  --config vite.media.config.ts \
  --port 5180 --strictPort
Stop other builds, browser tests, emulators, and similar workloads before measuring. The measurement starts the app at localhost:5184, so ports 5180 and 5184 must be available.
pnpm --filter @showcase/e2e e2e:performance

One full warm-up is excluded, followed by three measured runs in fresh browser contexts, executed serially at 1440 x 900. Set PERF_RUNS=5, for example, to choose one to ten measured runs. Adaptive quality remains enabled and the chosen video dimensions are recorded. Ordinary measurements use no CPU/network throttling or forced garbage collection.

Results are saved to tests/e2e/test-results/lifecycle-performance.json. They include individual samples, medians, ranges, browser/Node versions, CPU and memory information, and hashes identifying the code actually served. The app uses a development server, so this is not a production-page performance score.
What CPU and memory counters mean

rows: CPU time across the renderer process; excludes separate browser and GPU processes
Elapsed time in renderer tasks; not interchangeable with CPU time
JavaScript-managed objects; excludes total media-buffer, decoder, and GPU memory
Page objects and event handlers; may include detached objects awaiting collection
Resident pages by browser process type; includes shared pages and native allocations

blocks.text: One MiB is 1,048,576 bytes. A high final heap value alone does not establish a leak. Examine repeated runs, connected elements, and Player/UI ownership together. Correctness checks are enforced, but the suite does not impose arbitrary CPU or heap pass/fail thresholds.

For retention diagnosis, PERF_DIAGNOSTIC_GC=1 explicitly requests garbage collection after the final measured sample. Those results are recorded separately in collectionDiagnostics. They do not represent ordinary playback memory use or establish a CPU improvement.
Performance comparison recorded on 2026-10-21

Player 8.281.0 and UI 4.23.0 ran before and after the ownership correction on Apple M5, ten logical CPUs, 32 GiB RAM, Darwin 27.0.0, Node 24.19.0 and Chrome 155.0.8059.85. Each condition used one excluded full warm-up and three fresh contexts, one worker and zero retries. Adaptive quality selected the same 180p and 360p stages.

CPU times increased. The comparison does not isolate the cause of that increase. Ordinary heap samples depend on collection timing. Individual samples, ranges, hashes and process counts are in the linked measurement documentation.

After explicit garbage collection, retained JavaScript heap fell about 32%, DOM nodes 80% and listeners 96%. Process RSS increased. RSS includes shared pages, code and native allocations; it is not a private-allocation total. GPU-process RSS is system RAM, not VRAM. Both conditions had 988 connected elements, no live Player/media element, seven created and destroyed Players, no pending source/request and a stopped app timer. This does not establish total-memory savings, CPU improvement, leak freedom or long-session behavior.

Dynamic settings item labels and recommendation title/duration labels are owned outside the normal child tree. They now participate in exactly-once disposal. Source-change callbacks are registered through the UI manager’s wrapped Player so manager disposal also removes those callbacks. Regression checks reproduce each retention path and verify the correction.

The earlier measurement records HEAD 80a02ed with temporary 8.281.0 package overrides and the harness; it is not a clean checkout of that revision. The corrected measurement records dee205b with clean committed measured inputs. Application/shared-UI source hashes match; harness changes added provenance checks without changing the workload. Each served development response has its own recorded hash.

For the fixed 60-second fixture, three alternating pairs after excluded warm-ups reduced median generation time from 1.389 s to 1.146 s and child CPU time from 6.093 s to 5.694 s. Peak child RSS increased from 74.65 MB to 77.41 MB. All 25 generator checks passed. Media bytes matched except generated HLS program-date-time values and measurement reports. A two-CPU/128-MiB budget-input smoke run chose one thread and generated valid media; it did not impose an operating-system resource limit.
Run the checks

pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
pnpm build
bash scripts/test-env-lib.sh
pnpm --filter @showcase/e2e e2e:public

Use e2e:features for feature media, e2e:pages for the generated Pages artifact, and e2e:finalization for controlled live finalization. The combined pnpm verify command also synchronizes environment settings and shared UI assets. Steps requiring unavailable native toolchains are skipped. Read the executed/passed/failed/skipped summary rather than relying on the exit code alone.
Verification recorded in the public documentation

The following results were recorded in the public documentation on 2026-10-19. They were not rerun for publication of this guide. Selections and execution conditions differ, so do not add the counts together as if they were a single suite.

blocks.text: Pages automated tests intercept Analytics ingress in advance. Checking a collector request attempt and its notice does not establish remote receipt or dashboard aggregation. Host licensing, real collection, and account aggregation are separate checks.

For HEVC, Chrome 155 and Chromium 149 reported supported, smooth, and powerEfficient as true for a 640 x 360, 24-frames-per-second, 500-kbit/s capability query. This is an estimate of support. The local media checks actually played H.264; these results do not establish HEVC decoding, audible synchronization, or measured hardware power consumption.

blocks.title: Check the API documentation version
blocks.text: Current dependencies are Player 8.281.0 and UI 4.23.0. The 2026-10-21 comparison above uses those versions. Check matching API references and repository types before changing settings.
